claim: Meisosomes are repeated folded structures at the interface of the aECM (the cuticle) and the epidermis.
source: Meisosomes are repeated folded structures at the interface of the aECM (the cuticle) and the epidermis (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by TEM images in Figure 1 showing the structures at the cuticle-epidermis interface.

claim: Meisosomes are not present on the basal side of the epidermis, nor in the seam cells, the rectal epithelia, nor in the pharynx.
source: They are not present on the basal side of the epidermis, nor in the seam cells, the rectal epithelia, nor in the pharynx (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by absence of meisosomes in TEM images of these regions.

claim: In adults, meisosomes typically comprised 4–10 closely apposed parallel folds of the plasma membrane.
source: In adults, meisosomes typically comprised 4–10 closely apposed parallel folds of the plasma membrane, although we observed some with up to 30-folds (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by TEM images showing the number of folds in Figure 1C.

claim: Most folds formed an indentation 200–400 nm deep.
source: Most folds formed an indentation 200–400 nm deep (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: Supported by measurements from TEM images in Figure 1C-G.

claim: The gap between each cytoplasmic-facing plasma membrane fold was 35 nm.
source: The gap between each cytoplasmic-facing plasma membrane fold was 35 nm, 75% wider than that between the folds made from cuticle-facing plasma membrane (20 nm) (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by high-magnification TEM measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The gap between the folds made from cuticle-facing plasma membrane was 20 nm.
source: The gap between each cytoplasmic-facing plasma membrane fold was 35 nm, 75% wider than that between the folds made from cuticle-facing plasma membrane (20 nm) (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by high-magnification TEM measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The cytoplasmic faces of the folds were free of ribosomes but contained dense material close to the plasma membrane, separated by a thin less electron-dense area.
source: The cytoplasmic faces of the folds were free of ribosomes but contained dense material close to the plasma membrane, separated by a thin less electron-dense area (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by high-magnification TEM images in Figure 1G showing the ultrastructure.

claim: Meisosomes were frequently found in close proximity to mitochondria (85%, n = 355).
source: Meisosomes were frequently found in close proximity to mitochondria (85%, n = 355) (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of TEM images showing mitochondria near meisosomes.

claim: Meisosomes of similar dimensions were observed in both transverse and longitudinal sections.
source: Although very variable in a single worm, meisosomes of similar dimensions were observed in both transverse and longitudinal sections (Table 1), consistent with a random orientation relative to the animal's antero-posterior axis.
evidence: Supported by measurements in Table 1 comparing transverse and longitudinal sections.

claim: Meisosomes have a random orientation relative to the animal's antero-posterior axis in adults.
source: Although very variable in a single worm, meisosomes of similar dimensions were observed in both transverse and longitudinal sections (Table 1), consistent with a random orientation relative to the animal's antero-posterior axis.
evidence: Inferred from the similar dimensions in different section orientations and confirmed by freeze-fracture images.

claim: The random orientation of meisosomes was clearly visible in electron micrographs of freeze-fractured samples.
source: This random orientation was clearly visible in electron micrographs of freeze-fractured samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by freeze-fracture EM images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: In moulting larvae, meisosomes were in-between the position of circumferential furrows.
source: It contrasted with a much more regular pattern in moulting larvae, in which meisosomes were in-between the position of circumferential furrows, (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by TEM images of moulting larvae in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Some much smaller meisosomes, typically with only 2–4 shallow folds, were seen in the thin epidermal tissue that lies between body-wall muscles and the cuticle.
source: Some much smaller meisosomes, typically with only 2–4 shallow folds, were seen in the thin epidermal tissue that lies between body-wall muscles and the cuticle (dorsal and ventral epidermis, see Figure 1A) and that is largely devoid of cytoplasmic content (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by TEM images in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing smaller meisosomes.

claim: VHA-5 is one of four α-subunits of the transmembrane V0 complex of the vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase).
source: VHA-5, one of four α-subunits of the transmembrane V0 complex of the vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) (Oka et al., 2001; Pujol et al., 2001), and RAL-1, ortholog of human RALA (RAS like proto-oncogene A) (Frische et al., 2007), are the only known markers of meisosomes, with both proteins being also associated with multivesicular bodies (MVBs) that play a role in exosome secretion (Hyenne et al., 2015; Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Oka et al., 2001; Pujol et al., 2001).

claim: RAL-1 is an ortholog of human RALA (RAS like proto-oncogene A).
source: VHA-5, one of four α-subunits of the transmembrane V0 complex of the vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) (Oka et al., 2001; Pujol et al., 2001), and RAL-1, ortholog of human RALA (RAS like proto-oncogene A) (Frische et al., 2007), are the only known markers of meisosomes, with both proteins being also associated with multivesicular bodies (MVBs) that play a role in exosome secretion (Hyenne et al., 2015; Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frische et al., 2007.

claim: VHA-5 and RAL-1 are the only known markers of meisosomes.
source: VHA-5, one of four α-subunits of the transmembrane V0 complex of the vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) (Oka et al., 2001; Pujol et al., 2001), and RAL-1, ortholog of human RALA (RAS like proto-oncogene A) (Frische et al., 2007), are the only known markers of meisosomes, with both proteins being also associated with multivesicular bodies (MVBs) that play a role in exosome secretion (Hyenne et al., 2015; Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated as current knowledge based on cited literature.

claim: VHA-5 and RAL-1 are also associated with multivesicular bodies (MVBs) that play a role in exosome secretion.
source: VHA-5, one of four α-subunits of the transmembrane V0 complex of the vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) (Oka et al., 2001; Pujol et al., 2001), and RAL-1, ortholog of human RALA (RAS like proto-oncogene A) (Frische et al., 2007), are the only known markers of meisosomes, with both proteins being also associated with multivesicular bodies (MVBs) that play a role in exosome secretion (Hyenne et al., 2015; Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hyenne et al., 2015 and Liégeois et al., 2006.

claim: A TEM/immunogold staining study showed that more than 85% of the VHA-5 signal can be attributed to meisosomes.
source: A TEM/immunogold staining study showed that more than 85% of the VHA-5 signal can be attributed to meisosomes (Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liégeois et al., 2006.

claim: VHA-5::GFP shows a punctate fluorescence at the apical surface of the lateral epidermis, and in the ventral and dorsal ridges, from the head to the tail.
source: In all the strains, and in line with previous reports (Liégeois et al., 2006), we observed the same punctate fluorescence at the apical surface of the lateral epidermis, and in the ventral and dorsal ridges, from the head to the tail.
evidence: Supported by observations in multiple VHA-5 reporter strains and citation to Liégeois et al., 2006.

claim: VHA-5::GFP fluorescence is almost completely absent from the dorsal and ventral epidermis above the body-wall muscles, and underneath the seam cells.
source: As expected, it was almost completely absent from the dorsal and ventral epidermis above the body-wall muscles, and underneath the seam cells (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 3A-C showing the distribution pattern.

claim: Hemidesmosomes and meisosomes are present in complementary and non-overlapping regions of the epidermis.
source: By combining a MUP-4::GFP (Suman et al., 2019) and a VHA-5::RFP reporter (Liégeois et al., 2006), we confirmed the complementary pattern in the epidermis of hemidesmosomes above the muscles, and meisosomes in the lateral epidermis and dorso/ventral ridges (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by dual-labeling confocal images in Figure 3D showing non-overlapping patterns.

claim: VHA-5-marked structures have an irregular shape in no preferred direction in the lateral epidermis.
source: Higher resolution analysis in the lateral epidermis revealed the VHA-5-marked structures to have an irregular shape in no preferred direction in the lateral epidermis, consistent with the TEM and SBF-SEM analyses (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by high-resolution confocal images in Figure 3E and consistency with EM data.

claim: There is essentially no co-localisation between VHA-5::GFP and HGRS-1::mScarlet.
source: When we examined worms co-expressing VHA-5::GFP and HGRS-1::mScarlet, a known marker of MVBs and the endosome degradation pathway (Liégeois et al., 2006; Norris et al., 2017; Roudier et al., 2005; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2020), we observed essentially no co-localisation.
evidence: Supported by dual-labeling confocal imaging showing distinct patterns.

claim: The patterns of VHA-5::GFP and HGRS-1::mScarlet are distinct, with HGRS-1::mScarlet labelling structures that are less apical, larger and more scattered than those labelled by VHA-5::GFP.
source: Further, the patterns of the two markers were distinct, with HGRS-1::mScarlet labelling structures that were less apical, larger and more scattered that those labelled by VHA-5::GFP (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by confocal images comparing the two markers in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is no co-localisation between VHA-5::GFP and SNX-1::mScarlet, a marker for the recycling endosomes.
source: We also did not observe any co-localisation between VHA-5::GFP and SNX-1::mScarlet, a marker for the recycling endosomes, nor with LGG-1::mScarlet, an autophagolysosome marker (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by dual-labeling confocal images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is no co-localisation between VHA-5::GFP and LGG-1::mScarlet, an autophagolysosome marker.
source: We also did not observe any co-localisation between VHA-5::GFP and SNX-1::mScarlet, a marker for the recycling endosomes, nor with LGG-1::mScarlet, an autophagolysosome marker (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by dual-labeling confocal images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The plasma membrane of the epidermis in young adult worms contains heterogeneous macrodomains that can be revealed with a prenylated, or a pleckstrin homology domain-tagged form of GFP (GFP::CAAX and GFP::PH-PLC1δ, respectively).
source: We have previously shown that the plasma membrane of the epidermis in young adult worms contains heterogeneous macrodomains that can be revealed with a prenylated, or a pleckstrin homology domain-tagged form of GFP (GFP::CAAX and GFP::PH-PLC1δ, respectively) (Taffoni et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Taffoni et al., 2020).

claim: In worms co-expressing VHA-5::RFP and either GFP::CAAX or GFP::PH-PLC1δ, there is a high degree of co-localisation.
source: Interestingly, in worms co-expressing VHA-5::RFP and either one of these membrane probes, we observed a high degree of co-localisation (Figure 3G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by dual-labeling confocal images and quantification in Figure 3G, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: VHA-5 is primarily a marker of subdomains of the plasma membrane.
source: This further reinforces the notion that VHA-5 is primarily a marker of subdomains of the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the high co-localisation with plasma membrane markers and lack of co-localisation with vesicular markers.

claim: The fluorescence foci from VHA-5::GFP matched meisosomes as confirmed by CLEM.
source: After alignment of the confocal and TEM images, we could show that the fluorescence foci matched meisosomes (Figure 3I and J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by CLEM analysis shown in Figure 3I, J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The VHA-5::GFP signal observed at the apical membrane in the epidermis corresponds to meisosomes.
source: Together with previous CLEM observations in the excretory duct (Kolotuev et al., 2009), these results indicate that the VHA-5::GFP signal that we observe at the apical membrane in the epidermis corresponds to meisosomes and that VHA-5::GFP can be used in vivo as a bona fide meisosome marker for this study.
evidence: Supported by CLEM data in this study and citation to Kolotuev et al., 2009.

claim: VHA-5 has an essential role in alae formation and secretion of Hedgehog-related peptides through exocytosis via MVBs.
source: VHA-5 has been shown to have an essential role in alae formation and secretion of Hedgehog-related peptides through exocytosis via MVBs, but not to be involved in secretion of the collagen DPY-7, nor in meisosome morphology (Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liégeois et al., 2006.

claim: VHA-5 is not involved in secretion of the collagen DPY-7.
source: VHA-5 has been shown to have an essential role in alae formation and secretion of Hedgehog-related peptides through exocytosis via MVBs, but not to be involved in secretion of the collagen DPY-7, nor in meisosome morphology (Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liégeois et al., 2006.

claim: VHA-5 is not involved in meisosome morphology.
source: VHA-5 has been shown to have an essential role in alae formation and secretion of Hedgehog-related peptides through exocytosis via MVBs, but not to be involved in secretion of the collagen DPY-7, nor in meisosome morphology (Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liégeois et al., 2006.

claim: No gene has been assigned a role in determining meisosome structure to date.
source: Indeed, to date, no gene has been assigned a role in determining meisosome structure.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap.

claim: VHA-5::GFP aligns parallel to the actin fibres in animals entering the L4/adult moult.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Liégeois et al., 2007), we observed that VHA-5::GFP aligns parallel to the actin fibres in animals entering the L4/adult moult, a stage we refer to here as 'late L4.'
evidence: Supported by observations in this study and citation to Liégeois et al., 2007.

claim: The parallel circumferential alignment of VHA-5::GFP can be observed at the beginning of the L4 stage, in L4.1 worms.
source: The parallel circumferential alignment of VHA-5::GFP could be observed at the beginning of the L4 stage, in L4.1 worms, but was then lost at the L4.2 stage.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of staged worms shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The parallel circumferential alignment of VHA-5::GFP is lost at the L4.2 stage.
source: The parallel circumferential alignment of VHA-5::GFP could be observed at the beginning of the L4 stage, in L4.1 worms, but was then lost at the L4.2 stage.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of staged worms shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The parallel circumferential alignment of VHA-5::GFP reappears progressively starting in the L4.3 stage, culminating between the L4.7 and L4.9 stages, just before the moult.
source: It reappeared progressively starting in the L4.3 stage, culminating between the L4.7 and L4.9 stages, just before the moult.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of staged worms shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The alignment of VHA-5::GFP before moulting is consistent with EM observations of meisosome alignment.
source: This is consistent with the EM observations of meisosome alignment before moulting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Consistency between fluorescence and EM observations supports the claim.

claim: Meisosomes align in between the furrows at the late L4 stage.
source: As revealed with one marker of a furrow collagen, DPY-7::GFP (Miao et al., 2020), in combination with VHA-5::RFP, meisosomes align in between the furrows at the late L4 stage (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by dual-labeling confocal images in Figure 4B.

claim: During the L4.7 stage, some DPY-7::GFP can be observed in small vesicles on the apical side of the epidermis, which could represent the ongoing secretion of furrow collagen at that stage.
source: Notably, during the L4.7 stage, some DPY-7::GFP can be observed in small vesicles on the apical side of the epidermis, which could represent the ongoing secretion of furrow collagen at that stage.
evidence: Observation from confocal imaging with speculative interpretation.

claim: DPY-7::GFP vesicles do not co-localise with VHA-5::RFP during the L4.7 stage.
source: Interestingly, these vesicles do not co-localise with VHA-5::RFP (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by dual-labeling confocal images in Figure 4B.

claim: The CAAX and PH-PLC1δ markers that co-localise with VHA-5 in young adult animals also align during the L4 stage.
source: We further show that the CAAX and PH-PLC1δ markers that co-localise with VHA-5 in young adult animals (Figure 3G and H) also align during the L4 stage, but other vesicular components, like the one marked by HGRS-1, SNX-1, or LGG-1 do not (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 4C and D showing alignment patterns.

claim: Vesicular components marked by HGRS-1, SNX-1, or LGG-1 do not align during the L4 stage.
source: We further show that the CAAX and PH-PLC1δ markers that co-localise with VHA-5 in young adult animals (Figure 3G and H) also align during the L4 stage, but other vesicular components, like the one marked by HGRS-1, SNX-1, or LGG-1 do not (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 4C and D showing lack of alignment.

claim: Meisosomes, together with specific membrane subdomains, align in between the furrow before moulting.
source: Thus, meisosomes, together with specific membrane subdomains, align in between the furrow before moulting.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the alignment observations of VHA-5 and membrane markers.

claim: Before moulting, there is profound reorganisation of the cytoskeleton in the lateral epidermis.
source: Before moulting, there is profound reorganisation of the cytoskeleton in the lateral epidermis.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Microtubules and actin fibres align in a series of circumferential bands that are not present in adults before moulting.
source: Microtubules and actin fibres align in a series of circumferential bands that are not present in adults (Castiglioni et al., 2020; Costa et al., 1997; Taffoni et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by observations in this study and citations to previous work.

claim: Meisosomes exhibit the same sequence of dynamic changes in alignment as microtubules and actin.
source: Interestingly, meisosomes exhibited the same sequence of dynamic changes in alignment as microtubules and actin.
evidence: Supported by comparison of imaging data for VHA-5, actin, and microtubules shown in Figure 5.

claim: After the moult, there is a concomitant loss of alignment of VHA-5, actin, and microtubules.
source: After the moult, there was a concomitant loss of alignment of VHA-5, actin, and microtubules, so that in wild-type adult animals, as described above, there was no clear overall pattern to the organisation of meisosomes, actin, or microtubules (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging in Figure 5 showing loss of alignment in young adults.

claim: RNAi of dpy-7 provokes a loss of meisosome alignment compared to the control in late L4 worms.
source: Compared to the control, RNAi of dpy-7 provoked a loss of meisosome alignment (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of VHA-5::GFP in dpy-7 RNAi worms shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A similar loss of meisosome alignment phenotype was observed in dpy-3 mutant worms.
source: A similar phenotype was observed in dpy-3 mutant worms; DPY-3 is another furrow collagen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging in dpy-3 mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of furrow collagens is associated with a disruption of the normal organised pattern of both actin fibres and microtubules from the L4.3 stage.
source: Strikingly, this loss of furrow collagens was also associated with a disruption of the normal organised pattern of both actin fibres and microtubules from the L4.3 stage (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of actin and microtubules in dpy-7 RNAi worms shown in Figure 5.

claim: It was previously proposed that the formation of actin fibres and microtubules in apposed circumferential bands plays an instructive role in positioning the furrows.
source: It was previously proposed that the formation of actin fibres and microtubules in apposed circumferential bands plays an instructive role in positioning the furrows (Costa et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Costa et al., 1997.

claim: Furrow collagens in the cuticle govern the alignment of the underlying cytoskeleton as development progresses into the final moult.
source: Our results suggest, on the contrary, that furrow collagens in the cuticle govern the alignment of the underlying cytoskeleton as development progresses into the final moult.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of furrow collagens disrupts cytoskeleton alignment.

claim: Furrow collagens are required to align both meisosomes and the actin-microtubule cytoskeleton.
source: Thus, furrow collagens appear to be required to align both meisosomes and the actin-microtubule cytoskeleton.
evidence: Conclusion based on the disruption of alignment in furrow collagen mutants/RNAi.

claim: Different classes of cuticular collagen exist that are expressed and form either furrows or annuli.
source: As previously mentioned, different classes of cuticular collagen exist that are expressed and form either furrows or annuli (Figure 6A; Cox and Hirsh, 1985; Cox et al., 1980; McMahon et al., 2003; Page and Johnstone, 2007; Thein et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and schematic in Figure 6A.

claim: Only the furrow-less mutants, in contrast to mutants of annuli collagens, exhibit an increased expression of the AMP reporter nlp-29p::GFP.
source: While mutants in these collagens all have a Dumpy (i.e. short and fat; Dpy) phenotype, only the furrow-less mutants, in contrast to mutants of annuli collagens, exhibit an increased expression of the AMP reporter nlp-29p::GFP (Dodd et al., 2018; Pujol et al., 2008b; Zugasti et al., 2014; Zugasti et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Dodd et al., 2018; Pujol et al., 2008b; Zugasti et al., 2014; Zugasti et al., 2016).

claim: Furrow collagens have been proposed to be part of a damage sensor that relays information about cuticle integrity to the epidermis.
source: This is one reason that furrow collagens have been proposed to be part of a damage sensor that relays information about cuticle integrity to the epidermis (Dodd et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dodd et al., 2018.

claim: The nlp-29p::GFP reporter is induced at the late L4 stage in the wild-type before the last moult when the cuticle is reshaping.
source: Interestingly, this reporter is also induced at the late L4 stage in the wild-type before the last moult when the cuticle is reshaping (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Miao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citation to Miao et al., 2020.

claim: Inactivation of all six furrow collagen genes (dpy-2, dpy-3, dpy-7, dpy-8, dpy-9, and dpy-10) provoked a marked and specific alteration in the pattern of VHA-5::GFP compared to control RNAi or to annuli collagen inactivation.
source: Compared to control RNAi or to annuli collagen inactivation (dpy-4, dpy-5 and dpy-13), inactivation of all six furrow collagen genes (dpy-2, dpy-3, dpy-7, dpy-8, dpy-9, and dpy-10) provoked a marked and specific alteration in the pattern of VHA-5::GFP.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The meisosomes' normal reticulated pattern is fragmented in furrow collagen mutants, as reflected by a decrease in their average size and Feret's diameter, and a >25% increase in their density.
source: The meisosomes' normal reticulated pattern was fragmented, as reflected by a decrease in their average size and Feret's diameter, and a >25% increase in their density (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of confocal images in Figure 6B and C.

claim: A similar fragmentation of meisosomes was observed with different VHA-5 reporter strains, and either following inactivation of the furrow collagen gene's expression with RNAi or in null mutants.
source: A similar fragmentation was observed with the different VHA-5 reporter strains, and either following inactivation of the furrow collagen gene's expression with RNAi or in null mutants (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data across multiple strains and conditions in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Inactivation of furrow collagen genes did not cause marked alteration in the patterns of LGG-1, HGRS-1, or SNX-1.
source: In contrast to VHA-5::GFP, we observed no marked alteration in their patterns, and there was still no overlap with VHA-5::GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Neither dpy-3 nor dpy-7 inactivation had any effect on the size and density of the vesicular pattern of EEA-1::GFP.
source: Further, neither dpy-3 nor dpy-7 inactivation had any effect on the size and density of the vesicular pattern of EEA-1::GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), a marker of early endosomes (Shi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by quantification of EEA-1::GFP in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Loss of furrow collagen gene leads to a substantial fragmentation of meisosomes, without affecting vesicular organelles in the epidermis.
source: Thus, loss of furrow collagen gene leads to a substantial fragmentation of meisosomes, without affecting vesicular organelles in the epidermis.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the specific effect on meisosomes but not on other organelles.

claim: Furrow collagens play an important and specific role in maintaining meisosome integrity.
source: This suggests that furrow collagens play an important and specific role in maintaining meisosome integrity.
evidence: Inferred from the specific fragmentation of meisosomes in furrow collagen mutants.

claim: The cuticle is connected, through the epidermis, to the underlying body-wall muscles via hemidesmosomes.
source: The cuticle is connected, through the epidermis, to the underlying body-wall muscles via hemidesmosomes.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge.

claim: Complete loss of hemidesmosomes causes a fully penetrant lethality.
source: The maintenance of hemidesmosome integrity is vital; their complete loss causes a fully penetrant lethality.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge.

claim: Partial loss of the hemidesmosome component MUA-3 causes the cuticle to detach above the muscles.
source: On the other hand, partial loss of the hemidesmosome component MUA-3 causes the cuticle to detach above the muscles (Bercher et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bercher et al., 2001.

claim: Hemidesmosomes cannot play a role in the attachment of the lateral epidermis and the dorso/ventral ridge to the cuticle.
source: This suggests that hemidesmosomes cannot play a role in the attachment of the lateral epidermis and the dorso/ventral ridge to the cuticle.
evidence: Inferred from the complementary distribution of hemidesmosomes and meisosomes.

claim: The meisosomes are significantly smaller in furrow collagen mutants compared with another Dpy mutant (dpy-13) or the wild-type.
source: Examination by TEM first confirmed that the meisosomes are significantly smaller in furrow collagen mutants compared with another Dpy mutant (dpy-13) or the wild-type, irrespective of the direction of the section, as both longitudinal and sagittal sections show the same phenotype (Figure 7A–D, Table 1 ,and Figure 1 for the wild-type).
evidence: Supported by TEM images and measurements in Figure 7A-D and Table 1.

claim: In all furrow collagen mutants examined, there was a frequent disruption of the contact between the epidermal plasma membrane and the cuticle, either in the lateral epidermis or the dorso or ventral ridge, but not above the muscle quadrants.
source: In all furrow collagen mutants examined, there was a frequent disruption of the contact between the epidermal plasma membrane and the cuticle, either in the lateral epidermis or the dorso or ventral ridge, but not above the muscle quadrants (Figure 7B and G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by TEM images in Figure 7B, G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The detachment in furrow collagen mutants is clearly distinct from what is observed in Blister mutants where the detachment happens between the two main layers of the cuticle.
source: This detachment is clearly distinct from what is observed in so-called Blister mutants where, due to the absence of the connective struts, the detachment happens between the two main layers of the cuticle (Page and Johnstone, 2007).
evidence: Comparison with known phenotype from cited literature (Page and Johnstone, 2007).

claim: SBF-SEM analysis confirmed that the detachment between the cuticle and the epidermis was always found in the furrow collagen mutant outside the region of the body-wall muscles.
source: To confirm the phenotype, we analysed by SBF-SEM entire transversal worm sections over a length of 21.5 and 34.4 µm, for a wild-type and a dpy-2 mutant young adult worm, respectively. This confirmed that the detachment between the cuticle and the epidermis was always found in the furrow collagen mutant outside the region of the body-wall muscles (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: In furrow collagen mutants, the space between the cuticle and the underlying epidermal cell is often filled with a diverse range of cytoplasmic content, including membrane-bound vesicles with the appearance of endosomes, lysosomes, mitochondria, as well as electron-dense particles the size of ribosomes.
source: In furrow collagen mutants, the space between the cuticle and the underlying epidermal cell was often filled with a diverse range of cytoplasmic content, including membrane-bound vesicles with the appearance of endosomes, lysosomes, mitochondria, as well as electron-dense particles the size of ribosomes (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by TEM images in Figure 8A showing the contents of the detached space.

claim: In a dpy-3 furrow collagen mutant, GFP::CAAX and GFP::PH-PLC1δ are seen in numerous brightly stained vesicular structures that accumulate outside the epidermis at the level of the cuticular signal.
source: Compared to the wild-type, where the GFP signal is restricted to heterogeneous macrodomains in the plasma membrane (Taffoni et al., 2020), in a dpy-3 furrow collagen mutant, the GFP was seen in numerous brightly stained vesicular structures that accumulated outside the epidermis at the level of the mScarlet cuticular signal (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by live imaging with dual markers in Figure 8B.

claim: The meisosomes may play an important role in attaching the cuticle to the underlying epidermal cell.
source: Together, these phenotypes lead us to hypothesise that the meisosomes may play an important role in attaching the cuticle to the underlying epidermal cell and that loss of this intimate connection causes a profound alteration of epidermal integrity.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the detachment phenotype in furrow mutants with fragmented meisosomes.

claim: Loss of the intimate connection between cuticle and epidermis causes a profound alteration of epidermal integrity.
source: Together, these phenotypes lead us to hypothesise that the meisosomes may play an important role in attaching the cuticle to the underlying epidermal cell and that loss of this intimate connection causes a profound alteration of epidermal integrity.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the observed phenotypes in furrow mutants.

claim: Furrows are stiffer than the rest of the cuticle in wild-type worms.
source: It was previously shown that furrows are stiffer than the rest of the cuticle in wild-type worms (Essmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Essmann et al., 2016.

claim: Topographic AFM imaging provided further corroboration that in the absence of furrow collagens the cuticle has a disorganised aspect with irregular folds, lacking the usual repeated linear pattern of annuli and furrows.
source: While topographic AFM imaging (Figure 9A) provided further corroboration of the fact that in the absence of furrow collagens the cuticle has a disorganised aspect with irregular folds, lacking the usual repeated linear pattern of annuli and furrows, force spectroscopy AFM revealed differences in stiffness.
evidence: Supported by AFM topography images in Figure 9A.

claim: The non-furrow dpy-13 mutant has a rigidity similar to wild-type.
source: In contrast to the non-furrow dpy-13 mutant that had a rigidity similar to wild-type, the different dpy furrow mutants (dpy-2, dpy-3, dpy-7, and dpy-8) exhibited markedly less steep force-indentation curves (Figure 9B), and hence lower stiffness or Young's moduli (Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by AFM force spectroscopy data in Figure 9B and C.

claim: The different dpy furrow mutants (dpy-2, dpy-3, dpy-7, and dpy-8) exhibit markedly less steep force-indentation curves and hence lower stiffness or Young's moduli.
source: In contrast to the non-furrow dpy-13 mutant that had a rigidity similar to wild-type, the different dpy furrow mutants (dpy-2, dpy-3, dpy-7, and dpy-8) exhibited markedly less steep force-indentation curves (Figure 9B), and hence lower stiffness or Young's moduli (Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by AFM force spectroscopy data in Figure 9B and C.

claim: Furrow collagens are required for normal stiffness.
source: This suggests that furrow collagens are required for normal stiffness.
evidence: Inferred from the decreased stiffness in furrow collagen mutants.

claim: The effect on stiffness is a consequence of the fact that furrow collagens are essential for the presence of normal meisosomes.
source: While lack of certain collagens in the cuticle could directly affect cuticle stiffness, we hypothesise that the effect on stiffness is a consequence of the fact that furrow collagens are essential for the presence of normal meisosomes.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Meisosomes are composed of stacked parallel folds of the epidermal plasma membrane, alternately filled with cuticle.
source: We show that meisosomes are composed of stacked parallel folds of the epidermal plasma membrane, alternately filled with cuticle.
evidence: Supported by TEM and tomography data showing the structure.

claim: Just as hemidesmosomes connect the dorsal and ventral epidermis, above the muscles, to the cuticle, meisosomes connect the lateral epidermis to it.
source: We propose that just as hemidesmosomes connect the dorsal and ventral epidermis, above the muscles, to the cuticle, meisosomes connect the lateral epidermis to it.
evidence: Proposed based on the complementary distribution and the detachment phenotype in furrow mutants.

claim: Furrow mutants present marked modifications of the biomechanical properties of their skin.
source: Moreover, furrow mutants present marked modifications of the biomechanical properties of their skin and exhibit a constitutive damage response in the epidermis.
evidence: Supported by AFM measurements and previous reports of AMP gene expression.

claim: Furrow mutants exhibit a constitutive damage response in the epidermis.
source: Moreover, furrow mutants present marked modifications of the biomechanical properties of their skin and exhibit a constitutive damage response in the epidermis.
evidence: Supported by previous reports of increased AMP gene expression cited in the manuscript.

claim: Meisosomes co-localise to macrodomains enriched in phosphatidylinositol (4,5) bisphosphate.
source: As meisosomes co-localise to macrodomains enriched in phosphatidylinositol (4,5) bisphosphate, they could conceivably act, like eisosomes, as signalling platforms, to relay tensile information from the aECM to the underlying epidermis, as part of an integrated stress response to damage.
evidence: Supported by co-localisation with PH-PLC1δ marker shown in the study.

claim: Meisosomes could conceivably act, like eisosomes, as signalling platforms, to relay tensile information from the aECM to the underlying epidermis, as part of an integrated stress response to damage.
source: As meisosomes co-localise to macrodomains enriched in phosphatidylinositol (4,5) bisphosphate, they could conceivably act, like eisosomes, as signalling platforms, to relay tensile information from the aECM to the underlying epidermis, as part of an integrated stress response to damage.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on similarity to eisosomes and PIP2 enrichment.

claim: In yeast, eisosomes are single invaginations of the plasma membrane underneath the aECM, the cell wall, responsible for detecting changes in nutrient availability, cell wall integrity and membrane tension.
source: In yeast, eisosomes, single invaginations of the plasma membrane underneath the aECM, the cell wall, are responsible for detecting changes in nutrient availability, but also cell wall integrity and membrane tension. They relay information primarily via BAR domain proteins to induce the appropriate responses to environmental changes (Appadurai et al., 2020; Lanze et al., 2020; Moseley, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on eisosomes (Appadurai et al., 2020; Lanze et al., 2020; Moseley, 2018).

claim: Eisosomes relay information primarily via BAR domain proteins to induce the appropriate responses to environmental changes.
source: In yeast, eisosomes, single invaginations of the plasma membrane underneath the aECM, the cell wall, are responsible for detecting changes in nutrient availability, but also cell wall integrity and membrane tension. They relay information primarily via BAR domain proteins to induce the appropriate responses to environmental changes (Appadurai et al., 2020; Lanze et al., 2020; Moseley, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on eisosomes (Appadurai et al., 2020; Lanze et al., 2020; Moseley, 2018).

claim: Nematodes lack eisosomes.
source: While nematodes lack eisosomes, the apical plasma membrane of the epidermis, which is in direct contact with the aECM (the cuticle), is characterised by localised regions of folds that can be observed by electron microscopy (Liégeois et al., 2006; White et al., 1986; Wood, 1988).
evidence: Statement of knowledge based on lack of orthologous components.

claim: The apical plasma membrane of the epidermis in C. elegans is characterised by localised regions of folds that can be observed by electron microscopy.
source: While nematodes lack eisosomes, the apical plasma membrane of the epidermis, which is in direct contact with the aECM (the cuticle), is characterised by localised regions of folds that can be observed by electron microscopy (Liégeois et al., 2006; White et al., 1986; Wood, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous EM studies (Liégeois et al., 2006; White et al., 1986; Wood, 1988).

claim: The term 'meisosomes' refers to these structures in reference to eisosomes in yeast, meaning multifold eisosomes.
source: Given their superficial similarity, we refer to these structures as meisosomes, for multifold eisosomes.
evidence: Definition provided by the authors.

claim: Eisosome-like structures are conserved throughout fungi, microalgae, and lichens.
source: Eisosome-like structures are conserved throughout fungi, microalgae, and lichens (Lee et al., 2015; Zahumensky and Malinsky, 2019), but there are no direct orthologues for core components, such as Pil1 or LSP-1, in animals.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015 and Zahumensky and Malinsky, 2019.

claim: There are no direct orthologues for core eisosome components, such as Pil1 or LSP-1, in animals.
source: Eisosome-like structures are conserved throughout fungi, microalgae, and lichens (Lee et al., 2015; Zahumensky and Malinsky, 2019), but there are no direct orthologues for core components, such as Pil1 or LSP-1, in animals.
evidence: Statement of knowledge based on sequence comparisons.

claim: Meisosomes with their multiple membrane invaginations are distinct from interfacial structures in non-nematode species.
source: Conversely, the meisosomes that we describe here in C. elegans, with their multiple membrane invaginations that individually are similar in appearance to eisosomes, are, to the best of our knowledge, distinct from interfacial structures in non-nematode species.
evidence: Statement based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Meisosomes are enriched in a PH-PLCδ marker, which is known to bind phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
source: Interestingly, we show here that they are enriched in a PH-PLCδ marker, which is known to bind phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) (Lemmon et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by co-localisation data in this study and citation to Lemmon et al., 1995.

claim: PIP2 has a major role in signal transduction and in regulating cellular processes including actin cytoskeleton and membrane dynamics.
source: PIP2 has a major role in signal transduction and in regulating cellular processes including actin cytoskeleton and membrane dynamics (Katan and Cockcroft, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Katan and Cockcroft, 2020.

claim: The PH-PLCδ marker rapidly reorganises upon wounding of the lateral epidermis.
source: Moreover, we have previously shown that the same PH-PLCδ marker rapidly reorganises upon wounding of the lateral epidermis (Taffoni et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Taffoni et al., 2020).

claim: Inactivation of ral-1 did not eliminate VHA-5::GFP fluorescence in the epidermis.
source: Notably, inactivation of ral-1 did not eliminate VHA-5::GFP fluorescence in the epidermis (Hyenne et al., 2015), and knocking down the expression of vha-5 did not affect the secretion of DPY-7 (Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hyenne et al., 2015.

claim: Knocking down the expression of vha-5 did not affect the secretion of DPY-7.
source: Notably, inactivation of ral-1 did not eliminate VHA-5::GFP fluorescence in the epidermis (Hyenne et al., 2015), and knocking down the expression of vha-5 did not affect the secretion of DPY-7 (Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liégeois et al., 2006.

claim: The V-ATPase on meisosomes is not involved in cuticle synthesis.
source: This suggests that the V-ATPase on meisosomes is not involved in cuticle synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of vha-5 knockdown on DPY-7 secretion.

claim: A recent study reported the isolation of mutants with an abnormal pattern of VHA-5::RFP in the epidermis but attributed this to a change in MVBs.
source: Notably, a recent study reported the isolation of mutants with an abnormal pattern of VHA-5::RFP in the epidermis but attributed this to a change in MVBs (Shi et al., 2022), despite a lack of substantial co-localisation with HGRS-1, a well-characterised MVBs marker, part of the ESCRT-0 complex that sorts endosomes to MVBs (Babst, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shi et al., 2022.

claim: Mutants with an abnormal pattern of VHA-5::RFP more likely affect meisosomes rather than MVBs.
source: Since previous studies (Liégeois et al., 2006), and the results presented here, show that VHA-5 is predominantly a marker of meisosomes, more so than of MVBs, these mutants with an abnormal pattern of VHA 5::RFP more likely affect meisosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the predominant localization of VHA-5 to meisosomes shown in this and previous studies.

claim: fln-2 encodes the F-actin cross-linking protein filamin.
source: Indeed, we hypothesise that the one gene that was characterised in detail (Shi et al., 2022), fln-2, which encodes the F-actin cross-linking protein filamin (Zhao et al., 2019), could actually be involved in the formation and/or maintenance of meisosomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: fln-2 could be involved in the formation and/or maintenance of meisosomes.
source: Indeed, we hypothesise that the one gene that was characterised in detail (Shi et al., 2022), fln-2, which encodes the F-actin cross-linking protein filamin (Zhao et al., 2019), could actually be involved in the formation and/or maintenance of meisosomes.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the abnormal VHA-5 pattern in fln-2 mutants.

claim: A fln-2 loss-of-function mutation has been serendipitously found in several C. elegans strains originating from different wild-type stocks.
source: Interestingly, a fln-2 loss-of-function mutation has been serendipitously found in several C. elegans strains originating from a different wild-type stocks (Zhao et al., 2019), so careful attention to genotypes will be needed in future work.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: The constant 35 nm spacing of meisosome plasma membrane folds is one of their defining features.
source: One of their defining features is the constant 35 nm spacing of their constituent plasma membrane folds.
evidence: Supported by TEM measurements shown in the study.

claim: The striking electron-dense material apposed to each side of the membrane on the cytoplasm-facing folds may contain specific structural protein that maintain the uniform width of each meisosome fold.
source: One possibility is that the striking electron-dense material that is apposed to each side of the membrane on the cytoplasm-facing folds, spaced less than 10 nm apart, will contain specific structural protein that maintain the uniform width of each meisosome fold and influence their mechanical properties.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on the observed ultrastructure.

claim: The nematode cuticle is flexible enough to allow bending during locomotion.
source: Contrary to the cuticle of many adult insects, the nematode cuticle is flexible enough to allow bending during locomotion.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge.

claim: The nematode cuticle is thought to stretch to accommodate growth between moults.
source: It is also thought to stretch to accommodate growth between moults.
evidence: Statement of current understanding in the field.

claim: The circumferential furrows of the new cuticle appear exactly in register with the position of old furrows.
source: When the old cuticle is shed, it leaves in its place the new cuticle that had been moulded underneath it. The circumferential furrows of the new cuticle thus appear exactly in register with the position of old furrows.
evidence: Statement of observed phenomenon.

claim: Before moulting, the cytoskeleton aligns in the apical epidermis, underneath, and parallel to each furrow.
source: Before moulting, the cytoskeleton aligns in the apical epidermis, underneath, and parallel to each furrow.
evidence: Statement of observed phenomenon supported by citations.

claim: It was proposed that cytoskeleton alignment is important for positioning the furrows of the new cuticle.
source: Although this had been proposed to be important for positioning the furrows of the new cuticle (Costa et al., 1997; McMahon et al., 2003; Page and Johnstone, 2007), a recent study found unexpectedly that actin is dispensable for the alignment of furrows (Katz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costa et al., 1997; McMahon et al., 2003; Page and Johnstone, 2007.

claim: A recent study found that actin is dispensable for the alignment of furrows.
source: Although this had been proposed to be important for positioning the furrows of the new cuticle (Costa et al., 1997; McMahon et al., 2003; Page and Johnstone, 2007), a recent study found unexpectedly that actin is dispensable for the alignment of furrows (Katz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Katz et al., 2018.

claim: Only the old furrows are required to pattern the new furrows.
source: We propose therefore that only the old furrows are required to pattern the new furrows.
evidence: Proposed based on the finding that furrows determine cytoskeleton alignment.

claim: The LPR-3 protein that is part of the transient pre-cuticle is absent from the region of the furrows.
source: Consistent with such a model, the LPR-3 protein that is part of the transient pre-cuticle that is formed between the old and the new cuticles before each moult is absent from the region of the furrows (Forman-Rubinsky et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forman-Rubinsky et al., 2017.

claim: The alignment of meisosomes could result from steric constraints during moulting, in the limited space between nascent furrows of the new cuticle and the closely apposed circumferential actin fibres.
source: It could result from steric constraints during moulting, in the limited space between nascent furrows of the new cuticle and the closely apposed circumferential actin fibres.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed alignment.

claim: The alignment of meisosomes is not seen for vesicular organelles like MVBs, endosome, or autophagosomes.
source: It should, however, be noted that this alignment is not seen for vesicular organelles like MVBs, endosome, or autophagosomes.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data showing lack of alignment for these markers.

claim: The multiple folds of plasma membrane in meisosomes increase its contact surface with the cuticle thus ensuring a more robust connection of the aECM to the lateral epidermis.
source: Although this fragmentation could be a consequence of the detachment, we favour the converse hypothesis that fragmentation causes the detachment, and that the multiple folds of plasma membrane normally increase its contact surface with the cuticle thus ensuring a more robust connection of the aECM to the lateral epidermis.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: Hemidesmosomes secure the muscles to the cuticle through epidermis and are indispensable for worm development and viability.
source: These latter structures secure the muscles to the cuticle through epidermis and are indispensable for worm development and viability.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge.

claim: Above the muscles, the epidermis is extremely thin, with the apical and basal plasma membranes juxtaposed, linked via intermediate filaments that bridge apical and basal hemidesmosome protein complexes.
source: Above the muscles, the epidermis is extremely thin, with the apical and basal plasma membranes juxtaposed, linked via intermediate filaments that bridge apical and basal hemidesmosome protein complexes (Zhang and Labouesse, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang and Labouesse, 2010.

claim: MUA-3 is a hemidesmosome transmembrane protein in direct contact with the cuticle.
source: MUA-3 is a hemidesmosome transmembrane protein in direct contact with the cuticle.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge.

claim: In hypomorphic mua-3 mutants, large gaps form between the apical epidermal surface and the cuticle in the dorsoventral quadrants.
source: In hypomorphic mua-3 mutants, large gaps form between the apical epidermal surface and the cuticle in the dorsoventral quadrants, reflecting a loss of attachment of apical hemidesmosomes to the cuticle.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bercher et al., 2001.

claim: In mua-3(rh195) worms, the spaces between cuticle and epidermis appear devoid of contents, and the apical epidermal membrane is intact.
source: Unlike the cytoplasm-filled gaps we observed in furrowless mutants, in mua-3(rh195) worms, these spaces appear devoid of contents, and the apical epidermal membrane is intact (Bercher et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bercher et al., 2001.

claim: Fragmentation of meisosomes in furrowless mutants affects the integrity of the apical epidermal membrane in the lateral epidermis.
source: So, in contrast to the loss of hemidesmosomes, fragmentation of meisosomes in furrowless mutants affects the integrity of the apical epidermal membrane in the lateral epidermis, potentially explaining the permeability phenotype of furrowless mutants (Sandhu et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from the cytoplasm-filled gaps and citation to permeability phenotype (Sandhu et al., 2021).

claim: Both meisosomes in the lateral epidermis, and hemidesmosomes in the dorsoventral quadrants, have an analogous function, ensuring the attachment of the apical plasma membrane to the cuticle.
source: Despite these differences, both meisosomes in the lateral epidermis, and hemidesmosomes in the dorsoventral quadrants, do appear to have an analogous function, ensuring the attachment of the apical plasma membrane to the cuticle.
evidence: Proposed based on the complementary distribution and attachment phenotypes.

claim: In animals, ECMs provide mechanical support for tissue assembly and organ shape.
source: In animals, ECMs provide mechanical support for tissue assembly and organ shape.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge.

claim: During embryogenesis in C. elegans, the aECM is essential during elongation as it maintains embryonic integrity and relays mechanical stress produced by the actomyosin cytoskeleton and the muscles.
source: During embryogenesis in C. elegans, the aECM is essential during elongation as it not only maintains embryonic integrity, but also relays the mechanical stress produced by the actomyosin cytoskeleton and the muscles (Vuong-Brender et al., 2017a; Vuong-Brender et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vuong-Brender et al., 2017a and 2017b.

claim: Furrow Dpy mutants have a higher internal concentration of glycerol.
source: Furrow Dpy mutants are known to have a higher internal concentration of glycerol (Wheeler and Thomas, 2006), which will decrease their internal hydrostatic pressure.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wheeler and Thomas, 2006.

claim: The decreased hydrostatic pressure in furrow Dpy mutants is a consequence of the decrease in the stiffness of the cuticle.
source: We propose that this decreased hydrostatic pressure is a consequence of the decrease in the stiffness of the cuticle.
evidence: Proposed by the authors based on the measured decrease in stiffness.

claim: A decrease in stiffness and an increase in the activity of innate immune signalling pathways in the epidermis are signatures of ageing in C. elegans.
source: It is interesting to note, however, that a decrease in stiffness and an increase in the activity of innate immune signalling pathways in the epidermis are signatures of ageing in C. elegans (Lezi et al., 2018; Essmann et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lezi et al., 2018 and Essmann et al., 2020.
